topics.title: Nervous-system divisions and receptors
topics.summary: Central = control center. Peripheral = connecting paths. Enteric = intestine.
details: CNS: Brain and spinal cord: integrate sensory input, process information, and coordinate motor commands.
PNS: Nervous tissue outside the CNS and ENS in this textbook’s framing. Cranial and spinal nerves connect the CNS with peripheral tissues.
ENS: Neuronal networks in the digestive-tract walls. Can coordinate local visceral reflexes; sympathetic and parasympathetic activity influence them.
BIG DISTINCTION: Anatomical divisions describe structures. Functional divisions describe what information travels through those structures.
AFFERENT / SENSORY: Receptors send information toward the CNS: special senses, somatic sensation, and visceral sensation.
EFFERENT / MOTOR: Commands leave the CNS for effectors. “Motor” includes muscles and glands—not just visible movement.
SOMATIC MOTOR: Targets skeletal muscle. Includes voluntary movement and involuntary somatic reflexes.
AUTONOMIC MOTOR: Targets smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands, and adipose tissue. Sympathetic and parasympathetic are its major divisions.

topics.title: Neuron structure, transport and classifications
topics.summary: Dendrites receive; axon carries; terminals communicate.
details: INPUT REGION: Dendrites receive information. The cell body is the soma; the perikaryon is its cytoplasm around the nucleus.
TRIGGER REGION: Axon hillock is the transition from soma to axon. The initial segment is the key action-potential initiation region in the chapter’s model.
CONDUCTING REGION: Axon carries the action potential. Axolemma = axon membrane; axoplasm = axon cytoplasm.
OUTPUT REGION: Collaterals branch along an axon. Telodendria are fine terminal branches ending in synaptic terminals.
ANTEROGRADE: Kinesin carries material away from the cell body toward terminals along neurotubules.
RETROGRADE: Dynein carries material from terminals back toward the cell body.
ENERGY + SPEED: Transport uses ATP. The book gives fast transport up to 1,000 mm/day, averaging about 300; slow transport is a few mm/day.
WHY IT MATTERS: Terminals need proteins, enzymes and vesicle materials. Retrograde transport also returns debris and can carry harmful material toward the CNS.
ANAXONIC: Many processes but no obvious axon; found in the brain and special sense organs in the textbook.
BIPOLAR: One dendrite and one axon, with the soma between them; associated with special senses.
UNIPOLAR: A single process with the soma off to the side; typical sensory neurons of the PNS.
MULTIPOLAR: Many dendrites and one axon. Includes skeletal motor neurons and many CNS neurons; shape alone does not prove a motor function.
Sensory neuron | Peripheral receptor toward CNS | Cell bodies commonly in sensory ganglia
Motor neuron | CNS toward a peripheral effector | Somatic targets skeletal muscle; visceral targets other effectors
Interneuron | Integrates, distributes and coordinates signals | The chapter emphasizes interconnected CNS neurons

topics.title: Resting potential, pump and electrochemical gradients
topics.summary: Na+ mainly outside; K+ mainly inside; inside is negative at rest.
details: WHAT IS MEASURED?: The voltage inside the cell relative to outside—not an absolute amount of electricity in the cell.
ION DISTRIBUTION: Na+ is high outside; K+ is high inside. Intracellular negatively charged proteins also matter.
SELECTIVE PERMEABILITY: At rest, the membrane is more permeable to K+ than Na+. Leak channels remain open.
POLARIZED: A resting neuron has a charge separation and can respond to a stimulus; it is not currently firing an action potential.
TRANSPORT RULE: For one ATP used, the pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, against their concentration gradients.
WHY KEEP PUMPING?: Na+ leaks inward and K+ tends to leak outward. Pumping maintains the gradients that signaling requires.
NOT THE AP SWITCH: Rapid action-potential depolarization and repolarization occur through ion channels, not by the pump instantly moving the voltage up and down.
OVER TIME: The pump restores/maintains ion concentrations. Only a small fraction of ions moves during one action potential.
K+ | Out: concentration is higher inside | In: negative interior attracts it | Outward tendency, weakened by electrical pull
Na+ | In: concentration is higher outside | In: negative interior attracts it | Strong inward tendency
K+ EQUILIBRIUM: The book’s K+-selective thought experiment reaches approximately −90 mV, where the inward electrical force balances outward diffusion.
Na+ EQUILIBRIUM: In the Na+-permeable thought experiment, equilibrium is approximately +66 mV.
REAL RESTING MEMBRANE: The resting value is about −70 mV because real membranes have more than one ion pathway plus active maintenance.
IMPORTANT CAUTION: Do not learn “turn the pump off and the cell must become −90 mV” as a general rule. The textbook’s example assumes specific permeability conditions.

topics.summary: Chemical = key; voltage = charge; mechanical = stretch or push.
details: CHEMICALLY GATED: A ligand binds a receptor/channel. Example: ACh at the neuromuscular junction or a cholinergic synapse.
VOLTAGE GATED: A change in membrane potential alters the channel. Na+ and K+ channels support axonal action potentials; Ca2+ channels matter at terminals.
MECHANICALLY GATED: Physical deformation opens a channel, as in touch, pressure or vibration receptors.
LEAK CHANNEL: Different from the three gated categories: it is open at rest and contributes to resting conditions.
LOCATION: Common on dendrites and soma in the neuronal examples; the book also describes graded potentials in other cell types.
AMPLITUDE: A stronger stimulus produces a larger local change. There is no all-or-none threshold for the graded potential itself.
DISTANCE: The effect decreases as it spreads because of resistance and charge loss/spread; local current is passive.
DIRECTION: A graded potential can depolarize or hyperpolarize. It may or may not bring the axon’s initial segment to threshold.
DEPOLARIZATION: The membrane becomes less negative / more positive. −70 to −65 mV is depolarization even without an action potential.
REPOLARIZATION: Movement back toward the resting membrane potential after depolarization.
HYPERPOLARIZATION: The membrane becomes more negative than its resting value, such as −70 to −85 mV.
THRESHOLD: Your professor emphasizes approximately −55 mV at the initial segment. The book gives −60 to −55 mV and some figures use −60.

topics.title: Action potentials and refractory periods
topics.summary: Na+ IN brings voltage UP. K+ OUT brings voltage DOWN.
details: 1 | REACH THRESHOLD: A graded depolarization brings the trigger region to about −55 mV in the lecture example.
2 | Na+ ENTRY: Voltage-gated Na+ channels activate; rapid Na+ influx produces the rising phase and a peak around +30 mV.
3 | K+ EXIT: Na+ channels inactivate; voltage-gated K+ channels allow outward K+ movement, repolarizing the membrane.
4 | AFTER-HYPERPOLARIZATION: Delayed closure of K+ channels allows a brief undershoot before return toward −70 mV.
ABSOLUTE: From Na+ channel activation until recovery from inactivation: another action potential cannot be triggered in that membrane region.
RELATIVE: Some Na+ channels have recovered, but K+ conductance/hyperpolarization makes another action potential require a stronger-than-normal stimulus.
DIRECTION: The recently active membrane is refractory, helping the normal impulse travel toward excitable membrane ahead.
MAXIMUM FREQUENCY: The absolute refractory period limits how rapidly a neuron can fire again.

topics.title: Propagation, fiber types and stimulus intensity
topics.summary: Continuous = neighboring membrane sections take turns.
details: UNMYELINATED AXON: Local current from one active region depolarizes the next region of excitable membrane.
CHAIN REACTION: The next region reaches threshold, opens its voltage-gated Na+ channels, and generates another action potential.
NO FADING: Unlike a graded potential alone, the action potential is renewed along the axon.
ANALOGY: Each person in a line repeats the complete message to the next person; the message stays intact, but each relay takes time.
MYELINATED AXON: Myelin limits ion movement across internodal membrane.
NODE TO NODE: Local current travels beneath myelin and depolarizes the next node to threshold; the action potential is regenerated there.

topics.title: Postsynaptic potentials, summation and presynaptic regulation
topics.summary: EPSP = easier. IPSP = inhibited. Neither is itself an axonal AP.
details: EPSP: Excitatory postsynaptic potential: a graded depolarization that makes reaching threshold more likely.
IPSP: Inhibitory postsynaptic potential: the chapter’s example is graded hyperpolarization, making threshold harder to reach.
CHANNEL EXAMPLES: Na+ entry can depolarize. K+ exit can hyperpolarize; the book’s transmitter table also includes inhibitory Cl− channels.
NET EFFECT: A neuron integrates simultaneous excitatory and inhibitory input. The balance at the trigger region matters.
TEMPORAL: Repeated input at one synapse arrives close enough in time that a new effect adds to the previous one.
SPATIAL: Inputs from multiple synapses arrive together and combine across locations.
WHAT SUMS?: Graded postsynaptic potentials—not the amplitude of action potentials.
THRESHOLD TEST: The combined effect must sufficiently depolarize the initial segment; inhibitory input may cancel some excitation.
SETUP: For this simplified exercise, rest is −70 mV, threshold is −55 mV, and the stated effects reach the trigger region.
EXAMPLE A: Three simultaneous +5 mV EPSPs give −55 mV: threshold is reached.
EXAMPLE B: Three +5 mV EPSPs plus one −5 mV IPSP give −60 mV: still below threshold.
EXAMPLE C: Starting at −85 mV, a +15 mV depolarization gives −70 mV—not an action potential.
INHIBITION EXAMPLE: An axoaxonic input releases GABA; Ca2+ entry at the target terminal is reduced, so less neurotransmitter is released.
FACILITATION EXAMPLE: An axoaxonic input involving serotonin prolongs/enhances Ca2+ entry, increasing transmitter release.
WHERE IS THE CHANGE?: At the presynaptic terminal before that terminal communicates across its main synapse.
COMPARE WITH IPSP: An IPSP describes the target cell’s graded postsynaptic response. Presynaptic inhibition changes how much transmitter arrives.

topics.summary: Find the deep anterior fissure first; then name every other part relative to it.
details: POSTERIOR: Posterior median sulcus is the shallower midline groove; posterior/dorsal horns lie toward it.
ANTERIOR: Anterior median fissure is the deeper midline indentation; anterior/ventral horns are on this side.
GRAY CENTER: Butterfly/H-shaped gray matter surrounds the central canal. Gray commissures bridge the two halves.
WHITE OUTSIDE: Posterior, lateral and anterior white columns surround the gray matter; the anterior white commissure crosses the midline.
POSTERIOR → ANTERIOR: Somatic sensory; visceral sensory; visceral motor; somatic motor.
SENSORY HALF: Posterior horn nuclei receive and integrate incoming information.
MOTOR HALF: Lateral horn nuclei contribute visceral motor output; anterior horn nuclei contribute somatic motor output.
EXAM CUE: The professor explicitly flagged the organization of this diagram as something students should know.
DORSAL / POSTERIOR ROOT: Sensory afferent fibers enter the spinal cord. The dorsal root ganglion contains their cell bodies.
VENTRAL / ANTERIOR ROOT: Motor efferent axons leave. Their cell bodies are in the CNS, so there is no equivalent ventral root ganglion.
SPINAL NERVE: After roots join, the spinal nerve contains both sensory and motor fibers.
RAMI: Posterior and anterior rami also contain mixed fibers. A posterior ramus is not the same structure as a posterior root.

topics.summary: Endo = each axon; peri = packet; epi = entire nerve.
details: ENDONEURIUM: Delicate connective tissue around individual axons.
PERINEURIUM: Connective tissue around a fascicle—a bundle of axons.

DESCENDING: Carry motor commands from brain toward spinal levels. The lecture uses corticospinal as an example.

DEFINITION: A skin territory supplied by a particular spinal nerve/root; the book depicts bilateral territories for a pair.
OVERLAP: Adjacent territories overlap, so the boundaries are not isolated hard lines.
APPLICATION: Sensory changes can help localize a nerve/root problem; the chapter uses shingles as a recognizable distribution example.

topics.title: Neuronal pools and five circuit patterns
topics.summary: Diverge = distribute. Converge = collect. Serial = sequence. Parallel = simultaneous. Reverberate = repeat.

NEURONAL POOL: A functional group of interconnected neurons with particular input sources and output destinations.

topics.summary: Receptor → Sensory → Integration → Motor → Effector. “Receive, Send, Integrate, Move, Execute.”
details: 1 + 2 | INPUT: A stimulus activates a receptor; a sensory neuron carries the signal toward the CNS.
3 | INTEGRATION: Information is processed in the CNS. A polysynaptic arc uses interneurons; a monosynaptic arc can connect sensory directly to motor.
4 + 5 | OUTPUT: A motor neuron carries the command to a peripheral effector, which produces the response.
FAST PROTECTION: A spinal withdrawal response can start before conscious awareness of pain; collateral pathways also relay information to the brain.
How did it develop? | Innate / acquired | Inborn circuitry versus learned motor pattern
What is the effector? | Somatic / visceral | Skeletal muscle versus visceral effectors
How many synapses? | Monosynaptic / polysynaptic | One versus more than one synapse

MONOSYNAPTIC: Sensory neuron synapses directly on a motor neuron. Minimum two neurons, one CNS synapse.
POLYSYNAPTIC: One or more interneurons participate; multiple synapses enable excitation/inhibition of multiple muscle groups.
SPEED TRADEOFF: Fewer synapses minimize delay. More synapses allow more complex and adjustable responses.
COMMON TRAP: Five steps in a reflex arc do not mean five neurons or five synapses.

topics.title: Stretch, spindle, posture and tendon reflexes
topics.summary: Stretch a muscle → that muscle contracts. The receptor is the muscle spindle.
details: STIMULUS: A patellar-tendon tap briefly stretches quadriceps and its muscle spindles.
SENSORY ARM: The spindle’s sensory neuron enters through the dorsal root and excites a motor neuron.
MOTOR ARM: Motor output returns to the stretched muscle; quadriceps contraction extends the knee.
FUNCTION: Automatic opposition to stretch helps regulate muscle length and posture. The core excitatory arc is monosynaptic.
INTRAFUSAL: Specialized small fibers inside the spindle; a central sensory region is monitored by sensory endings.
EXTRAFUSAL: The surrounding ordinary skeletal muscle fibers that generate most muscle force.
GAMMA EFFERENTS: Motor axons to the contractile ends of intrafusal fibers; adjust spindle sensitivity.
WHY ADJUST?: As a muscle shortens, gamma activity helps keep the sensory region responsive to a newly imposed stretch or load.
UPRIGHT STANCE: Multiple muscle groups continually make small adjustments to keep the body balanced.
FORWARD LEAN: Stretching postural muscles can increase their contraction and counter the change in position.
COORDINATION: If correction overshoots, different muscle groups adjust; this is not one isolated, permanent contraction.
CONNECTION: The lecture connects proprioceptive input, neural pools and subconscious balance control to these ongoing responses.

Typical source response | Contract the stretched muscle | Inhibit the muscle generating excessive tension
